cells.seam: Is the naming 'Jesus the Nazarene, the crucified one' standing on the Isaianic suffering-servant identification of the righteous one who is 'cut off,' and if so does the messenger's identification-through-crucifixion preserve the servant's vindication-after-suffering pattern or reassign it to a single named figure?

The young man's promise that Jesus 'goes before you into Galilee' repeats Jesus' own pre-Passion prediction, but leaves unsaid whether the messenger's warrant derives from having heard Jesus or from independent angelic knowledge — the identity of source-sense (Jesus' prediction of post-resurrection reunion) and use-sense (fulfillment-announcement) is asserted by the 'as he told you' formula without accounting for how the messenger knows.

The clause 'as he said to you' explicitly anchors the present promise in Jesus' prior speech, but leaves unsaid the gap between a prediction spoken only to the disciples (not to the women) and its being relayed BY the women — the chain of transmission is asserted but not narrated.

Is the temporal marker 'early on the first day of the week' for the rising standing on the Hoseanic 'on the third day he will raise us up,' and if so does the shift from a communal covenant-restoration idiom to a single figure's dawn-resurrection preserve or reassign the source's sense?

The parenthetical 'from whom he had cast out seven demons' imports Mary Magdalene's back-story as established fact, but leaves unsaid whether the appended verses are drawing on Luke's tradition or on a shared pre-gospel notice — the identification is used to authorize her as first witness without narrating how the reader is expected to know it.

The brief notice that Jesus appeared 'in another form to two of them as they walked into the country' compresses the Emmaus episode into a summary, but leaves unsaid whether 'another form' is the compiler's own interpretation of the Lukan non-recognition motif or an independent tradition — the borrowing repackages a full narrative as a datum in a disbelief-sequence.

The appearance 'to the eleven as they sat at table' condenses the Lukan/Johannine table-appearance to the gathered disciples, but leaves unsaid whether the meal-setting is retained for its Lukan force (bodily eating as proof) or merely as a scene-marker — the borrowing keeps the setting while dropping the demonstration.

'Go into all the world' echoes the Matthean 'go therefore,' but leaves unsaid whether the geographic-universal frame ('all the world') is a fresh coinage or a re-cast of the Matthean ethnic-universal ('all nations').

The universal commission 'go into all the world and preach the good news to the whole creation' rhymes with the Matthean Great Commission's 'all nations,' but leaves unsaid whether 'whole creation' preserves the Matthean ethnic-universal sense or extends it cosmically — the borrowing enlarges the audience while retaining the commissioning form.

Is the binary 'whoever disbelieves will be condemned' standing on the Johannine judgment-formula in which the one who does not believe is already condemned, and if so does it preserve realized-condemnation or shift it into future-verdict?

The promise that believers 'will speak in new tongues' rhymes with the Pentecost narrative of the disciples speaking in other languages, but leaves unsaid whether 'new' preserves the Lukan sense of previously-unknown human languages given for cross-cultural proclamation or extends it toward a broader charismatic-speech phenomenon.

Is the promise 'they will take up serpents' standing on the Malta episode where Paul shakes off a viper unharmed, and if so does the borrowing generalize a one-time apostolic sign into a standing believer-charism?

The promise of hand-laying healing rhymes with apostolic healing practice, but leaves unsaid whether the gesture preserves the apostolic-office frame or extends the charism to every believer without distinction.

Is the notice that the Lord 'was received up into heaven' standing on the Elijah ascent, and if so does it preserve the prophet-taken-alive pattern or repurpose it as post-resurrection enthronement rather than escape from death?

The being-taken-up rhymes with the Lukan ascension notices, but leaves unsaid whether the borrowing preserves Luke's carefully-narrated ascension-scene or condenses it into a bare theological datum stripped of setting and witnesses.

'Sat down at the right hand of God' imports the royal-oracle image of the Davidic lord seated at YHWH's right, but leaves unsaid whether the enthronement's original sense — a king awaiting the subjection of enemies — is preserved as ongoing wait or collapsed into an accomplished vindication.

Is the notice that the Lord confirmed the word by accompanying signs standing on the Hebrews formula that God bore witness to the message by signs and wonders, and if so does the borrowing preserve God-as-attester or reassign the attesting to the risen Lord?
